args.text: [lane-heron] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to servers that have moved or been retired, causing failures. (2) Slow recovery: during an outage or failover, traffic keeps going to the dead address until the cache expires. (3) Prolonged poisoning: a forged or wrong answer stays in the cache longer, so harm lasts longer. Figures for typical cache lifetimes: unknown.

[lane-heron] Idempotent (safe to repeat with the same result) retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. Without idempotency, a retry could charge a customer twice or create duplicate records, whereas with it, repeating the request is harmless.

[lane-heron] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Leaked timing: the leading bits hold a creation timestamp, so anyone seeing an ID can estimate when the record was made, and that may be unwanted. (2) Size and ordering limits: at 16 bytes it is larger than a plain integer key, so indexes take more space, and IDs made within the same millisecond on different servers are only roughly ordered, not strictly.

[lane-heron] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a file where a database records each change before applying it to the main data, so the change is safely on disk first. If the system crashes, it replays the log on restart to recover completed changes and discard unfinished ones, keeping the data consistent.

[lane-heron] (1) Fair comparison: if the client version changes between runs, any difference in results could come from the client rather than the system being tested, so pinning isolates the one thing you mean to measure. (2) Reproducibility: others, or you later on, can rerun the benchmark and get comparable results, because new releases may alter speed, defaults or behaviour without notice.

[lane-heron] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal producers to slow down or stop when consumers cannot keep up, instead of letting the queue grow without limit. It can work by blocking or rejecting new items once the queue is full, which protects memory and keeps delays predictable.

[lane-heron] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on two machines, for example after scaling out or a failover; (2) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts, so the two overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a lock file or a database row lock, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

[lane-heron] A tombstone is a small marker written in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. Instead of removing the data at once, the store records that it was deleted, so every copy learns about the deletion and an out-of-date copy cannot bring the item back. Tombstones are removed only after a grace period, once all copies have had time to see them.

[lane-heron] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change, so rerunning it gives different results; (2) the failures depend on things unrelated to the code, such as timing, test order, shared state or network delays, so they appear at random and are hard to reproduce.

[lane-heron] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock only until a set expiry time. If the holder's clock runs slow compared with the lock service's clock, it believes its lease is still valid after the service has expired it and given the lock to someone else. Two holders then act at once, which the lock was meant to prevent. A clock that runs fast has the opposite problem: the holder gives up early and work is wasted. Safer designs measure durations with a steady local timer and add a fencing token, a rising number that the protected resource checks, so it can reject a stale holder.
